Business model design
Busy all month, nothing left at the end of it. Before you build anything, find out which assumptions your revenue stands on, and which one, if wrong, brings the whole thing down.
Busy is not the same as earning
Founders usually open with the website, or the product. A few questions in, the real gap shows: it isn't settled yet what's being sold, to whom, or at what price.
A model can look great on slides while nobody knows which wrong assumption would sink it. And because those assumptions live nowhere on paper, nobody tests them either. Decisions run on feel.

We're Roxana Negaresh and Arshia Amani. We start by writing the assumptions down and ranking them by how much damage each does if it's wrong. Then we rebuild the model around how the money actually flows, and design small tests for the riskiest ones, with continue-or-stop criteria fixed before a test starts. The numbers are calculations, not prophecies: every one sits next to the assumption behind it. It's the same habit as a written scope on a website project, and our real template is public: what is a project scope?
Who this helps

items: You want to know, before building, exactly which assumptions your revenue is standing on.
Money comes in, but you can't say which part of the business earns it and which part eats it.
You're weighing a big change, new pricing, a new market, and you'd rather test it small first.

blocks.html: Not what this is

items: You want a pitch deck to raise money. What we make can feed one, but it isn't one, and we won't pretend otherwise.
You want a forecast dressed up as a prediction. We build the calculation from your inputs and written assumptions, not a number that promises the future.
You need investment, legal or tax advice. This is none of those, honestly.

blocks.html: Three phases, in order

items: Diagnosis. Input: conversations with the founders and whatever sales and cost data exists. Output: an assumption map ranked by risk, meaning which assumption hurts most if it's wrong. Owner: dadmor with you.

Redesign. Input: the assumption map you approved. Output: the model rebuilt around its revenue logic, in a spreadsheet where every number links back to a written assumption. Owner: dadmor; approval: you.

Validation. Input: the redesigned model. Output: tests for the three riskiest assumptions, kill/continue criteria written before each one runs, and a log of results. Running the tests: you; designing and reading them: dadmor.

blocks.html: Deliverables
What changes the size

items: What sets the size of each phase: how many products or revenue streams, how many markets, and how much real data there is to work with.
From you: access to sales and cost data, whatever exists, your time for conversations, and running the tests.
What holds things up: data nobody can find, and tests launched before the criteria were written down.

blocks.html: How it's priced

items: Each phase gets its own fixed proposal. Start with Diagnosis alone if you like, and decide the rest afterwards.

blocks.html: The band is only a starting estimate, not a price. Each phase is priced on its own after the scoping conversation, in a written proposal.
The honest limits

items: Testing shrinks risk. It doesn't guarantee success, and sometimes the honest result is that the current model doesn't work. That's useful too.
Spreadsheet numbers are calculations, not predictions. Each one is only as solid as the assumption underneath it.
Running the tests is your job. If they never run, Validation stays a plan on paper.
